title: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb
sections: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb (Q1-Q100)

questions.text: The great saphenous vein is a major superficial vessel of the lower limb. How is this vein anatomically formed at its most distal point?
options: By the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot
By the continuation of the lateral marginal vein of the foot
By the confluence of the plantar venous network and the medial marginal vein
By the direct continuation of the anterior tibial vein across the ankle
questions.correctAnswer: A. By the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein originates on the medial aspect of the foot through the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: A patient presents with sudden calf swelling and a positive Homan's sign. The physician suspects a clot in the deep venous system. Which of the following is the most severe, potentially life-threatening complication of this condition?
questions.explanation: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) can lead to a pulmonary embolism (PE) if the clot breaks loose and travels to the lungs, making it a critical complication.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: During physical activity, blood in the deep veins of the leg is propelled toward the heart against gravity. Which mechanism is primarily responsible for this upward propulsion?
questions.explanation: The musculovenous pump involves the contraction of surrounding muscles within tight fascial compartments, which squeezes the deep veins and forces blood upward through one-way valves.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The external iliac artery is the primary source of arterial blood for the lower limb. At which specific anatomical landmark does it transition into the femoral artery?
questions.explanation: The external iliac artery officially changes its name to the femoral artery as it passes under the inguinal ligament to enter the femoral triangle.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Deep veins in the lower limb often present as paired, interconnecting vessels that flank an artery. What is the clinical and anatomical term for this specific venous arrangement?
questions.explanation: Venae comitantes are paired accompanying veins that wrap around an artery, utilizing the artery's pulsations within a shared sheath to assist venous return.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: To prevent the backflow of blood, the great saphenous vein is equipped with numerous valves. Approximately how many valves does this vein typically contain along its course?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein possesses 10-12 valves, which are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh, helping to break the blood column into shorter segments.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Perforating veins play a critical role in lower limb hemodynamics. What is their primary anatomical function?
options: To supply oxygenated blood to the deep fascia
To connect the anterior and posterior tibial venous systems
To allow blood to flow only from the superficial veins to the deep veins
questions.correctAnswer: D. To allow blood to flow only from the superficial veins to the deep veins
questions.explanation: Perforating veins penetrate the deep fascia and contain valves that ensure unidirectional blood flow from the superficial venous system into the deep venous system.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which superficial vein ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus and runs along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon?
questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein originates from the lateral side of the foot and ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus before moving up the posterior calf.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The profunda femoris artery gives rise to three main sets of branches. Which of these branches wraps around the posteromedial aspect of the femur to supply its head and neck?
questions.explanation: The medial femoral circumflex artery travels posteromedially and is the primary source of arterial blood to the head and neck of the femur.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The femoral artery traverses the anterior thigh and eventually enters the posterior compartment. Through which specific structure does it pass to become the popliteal artery?
questions.explanation: The adductor hiatus is an opening in the adductor magnus muscle through which the femoral artery passes to reach the popliteal fossa, where it becomes the popliteal artery.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: A fracture of the femoral neck is clinically significant due to the high risk of damaging the retinacular arteries. What is the primary complication resulting from this vascular damage?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Severe compartment syndrome of the thigh
Complete paralysis of the quadriceps femoris
Ischemic ulceration of the medial knee
questions.correctAnswer: A. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
questions.explanation: Because the medial circumflex femoral artery is the primary supply to the femoral head, a femoral neck fracture can tear these vessels, leading to bone death (avascular necrosis).
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which artery descends through the obturator canal to supply the pectineus, obturator externus, adductor muscles, and gracilis?
questions.explanation: The obturator artery arises from the internal iliac artery, passes through the obturator canal, and gives off an anterior branch that supplies these specific medial thigh muscles.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The superior gluteal artery exits the pelvis to enter the gluteal region. What is its precise anatomical relationship to the piriformis muscle as it exits the greater sciatic foramen?
options: It pierces the piriformis muscle directly.
It passes inferior to the piriformis muscle.
It passes medial to the piriformis muscle.
It passes superior to the piriformis muscle.
questions.correctAnswer: D. It passes superior to the piriformis muscle.
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal artery enters the gluteal region through the greater sciatic foramen strictly superior to the piriformis muscle.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The dorsalis pedis artery is the primary arterial supply to the dorsum of the foot. It is a direct distal continuation of which major leg artery?
questions.explanation: As the anterior tibial artery crosses the ankle joint into the foot, it continues under a new name: the dorsalis pedis artery.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which artery passes anteriorly through a gap in the superior part of the interosseous membrane to supply the anterior compartment of the leg?
questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery originates from the popliteal artery and immediately passes through the interosseous membrane to descend between the tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which major deep vein of the thigh joins the terminal portion of the femoral vein, draining blood from the thigh muscles via perforating veins?
options: Deep vein of the thigh (profunda femoris vein)
questions.correctAnswer: A. Deep vein of the thigh (profunda femoris vein)
questions.explanation: The deep vein of the thigh (profunda femoris vein) collects blood from the muscular perforating veins and empties directly into the terminal portion of the femoral vein.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The deep plantar arch of the foot is primarily formed by the lateral plantar artery. Which artery provides the deep plantar branch that completes this arch medially?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery gives off a deep plantar artery that pierces the first dorsal interosseous muscle to join and complete the deep plantar arch.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: When a clinician palpates the dorsalis pedis pulse, they typically locate it on the dorsum of the foot. The artery runs just lateral to the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis pulse is found just lateral to the prominent tendon of the extensor hallucis longus on the dorsal aspect of the foot.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The medial plantar artery splits into superficial and deep branches. Which specific musculature is primarily supplied by its deep branch?
options: Muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg
Muscles of the central plantar aponeurosis
questions.correctAnswer: D. Muscles of the great toe
questions.explanation: The medial plantar artery's deep branch is primarily responsible for supplying the muscles associated with the great toe.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: To evaluate the posterior tibial pulse, a clinician must palpate the artery in the ankle region. Where is this pulse most reliably found?
questions.correctAnswer: B. Inferoposterior to the medial malleolus
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery passes through the tarsal tunnel, making its pulse palpable in the groove inferoposterior to the medial malleolus.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: An aneurysm of the popliteal artery can compress adjacent structures within the popliteal fossa. Which nerve is most susceptible to this compression, potentially leading to weakened plantarflexion?
questions.explanation: The tibial nerve runs centrally through the popliteal fossa alongside the popliteal vessels. An expanding aneurysm here can compress it, affecting plantarflexion and foot sensation.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The superficial lymphatic vessels accompanying the great saphenous vein drain into a specific group of nodes in the groin. What is this group called?
options: Vertical group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes
questions.correctAnswer: A. Vertical group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes
questions.explanation: Lymphatics shadowing the great saphenous vein empty primarily into the vertical (inferior) group of the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Intermittent claudication is a classic symptom of Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD). Which clinical test is commonly used to assess the severity of this arterial occlusion?
questions.explanation: The Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) is a diagnostic test that compares the blood pressure in the ankle with that in the arm to evaluate the severity of PAD.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which lymph node cluster acts as the primary drainage site for the lymphatic vessels that accompany the small saphenous vein?
questions.explanation: The lymphatic vessels tracking with the small saphenous vein drain directly into the popliteal lymph nodes located within the popliteal fossa.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The deep inguinal lymph nodes receive lymph from the popliteal nodes and deep structures of the limb. Where are they anatomically situated?
options: Under the deep fascia on the medial aspect of the femoral vein
Superficial to the fascia lata near the saphenous opening
Along the course of the external iliac artery
questions.correctAnswer: A. Under the deep fascia on the medial aspect of the femoral vein
questions.explanation: The deep inguinal lymph nodes are positioned deeply, just under the deep fascia and specifically along the medial aspect of the femoral vein.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The genicular anastomosis provides critical collateral circulation around the knee. Which specific branch of the popliteal artery contributes to this network on the superomedial aspect?
questions.explanation: The superior medial genicular artery is a direct branch of the popliteal artery that wraps around the femur superior to the medial condyle.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: A patient presents with massive swelling of the lower limb due to a parasitic infection (filariasis). What is the specific medical term for this condition caused by lymphatic blockage?
questions.explanation: Lymphedema is the accumulation of interstitial fluid resulting from the blockage, damage, or removal of lymphatic vessels and nodes.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which artery arises directly from the femoral artery and descends superomedially to participate in the genicular anastomosis?
questions.explanation: The descending genicular artery branches off the femoral artery just before it passes through the adductor hiatus, contributing to the knee's collateral circulation.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The inferior gluteal artery leaves the pelvis to enter the gluteal region through the greater sciatic foramen. Where does it emerge relative to the piriformis muscle?
questions.explanation: The inferior gluteal artery passes out of the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen specifically below (inferior to) the piriformis muscle, supplying the gluteus maximus and posterior thigh.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The circumflex fibular branch joins the anastomoses around the knee. From which parent vessel does it typically originate?
questions.explanation: The circumflex fibular branch typically arises from the posterior tibial artery and winds laterally around the fibular neck.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The lateral circumflex femoral artery gives off a specific branch that descends to join the genicular anastomosis. What is the name of this branch?
options: Descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery
questions.correctAnswer: B. Descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery
questions.explanation: The lateral circumflex femoral artery has a descending branch that travels down the lateral thigh to anastomose with the superior lateral genicular artery at the knee.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which artery branches from the anterior tibial artery and travels superiorly to contribute to the inferolateral aspect of the genicular anastomosis?
questions.explanation: The anterior tibial recurrent artery ascends from the anterior tibial artery to join the peri-articular anastomosis around the knee joint.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which group of arteries perforates the aponeurotic portion of the adductor magnus attachment to supply the central portions of the hamstring muscles?
options: Perforating branches of the profunda femoris
questions.correctAnswer: C. Perforating branches of the profunda femoris
questions.explanation: The profunda femoris artery gives rise to three or four perforating arteries that piece the adductor magnus to enter the posterior compartment, serving as the primary blood supply for the hamstrings.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: In a coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) procedure, which lower limb vessel is frequently harvested due to its superficial location and uniform diameter?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein is highly accessible in the subcutaneous tissue and maintains a remarkably uniform diameter throughout its long course, making it the premier choice for autologous vascular grafts.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and external pudendal veins typically empty directly into which vessel near its termination?
questions.explanation: Just before piercing the saphenous opening to enter the femoral vein, the great saphenous vein receives several named tributaries from the groin region.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which superficial vein begins on the lateral side of the foot from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch?
questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein is formed laterally by the union of the dorsal venous arch and the dorsal vein of the 5th toe, ascending posterior to the lateral malleolus.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The great saphenous vein passes posterior to which prominent bony landmark of the knee region?
questions.correctAnswer: C. Medial condyle of the femur
questions.explanation: As the great saphenous vein ascends the medial side of the leg and thigh, it specifically passes roughly a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella, running directly posterior to the medial condyle of the femur.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Deep veins of the leg (anterior tibial, posterior tibial, and fibular veins) converge posterior to the knee to directly flow into which vessel?
questions.explanation: All three major paired deep veins of the leg drain proximally into the popliteal vein, which acts as the major deep venous conduit through the popliteal fossa.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The small saphenous vein ascends in the leg by passing between the heads of which muscle before penetrating the deep fascia?
questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein travels superficially up the midline of the posterior calf and then passes subfascially directly between the two bellies of the gastrocnemius muscle.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: In cases of melanoma on the lower limb, checking for metastasis involves a biopsy of the sentinel node. In which node group is the sentinel node for the lower limb most commonly found?
questions.explanation: Since almost all superficial lymphatics of the lower limb converge on the inguinal lymph nodes (superficial and deep), a sentinel lymph node biopsy to detect melanoma spread typically targets this groin region.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The genicular anastomosis is essential for providing collateral circulation to the leg. This bypass mechanism is particularly important when which artery is transiently kinked or occluded during full knee flexion?
questions.explanation: Full flexion of the knee can physically kink and compress the popliteal artery. The rich genicular anastomosis surrounding the joint ensures continuous blood flow to the leg despite this temporary main-vessel occlusion.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The lateral plantar artery arches medially across the foot to form the deep plantar arch. This arch gives rise to multiple branches, including which specific vessels that divide near the bases of the proximal phalanges?
questions.explanation: The deep plantar arch crosses the sole of the foot and gives rise to four plantar metatarsal arteries. These arteries travel distally and bifurcate into plantar digital arteries to supply the toes.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The internal pudendal artery enters the gluteal region through the greater sciatic foramen, descends posterior to the ischial spine, and enters the perineum through which structure?
questions.explanation: The internal pudendal artery takes a unique course, leaving the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen, hooking around the ischial spine, and immediately re-entering the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The superficial branch of the medial plantar artery supplies the skin on the medial side of the sole. Its more lateral digital branches typically anastomose with which vessels?
questions.explanation: The lateral digital branches of the superficial medial plantar artery anastomose with the medial plantar metatarsal arteries (which originate from the deep plantar arch) to complete the foot's vascular network.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Deep lymphatic vessels from the leg accompany deep veins and enter the popliteal lymph nodes. Most lymph from these nodes then ascends to directly drain into which node group?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the popliteal nodes travels up the thigh via deep lymphatic vessels to drain primarily into the deep inguinal lymph nodes located near the femoral vein.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: After exiting the femoral triangle, the femoral artery continues down the anterior aspect of the thigh through a specific tunnel. What is the name of this passage?
questions.explanation: The femoral artery leaves the femoral triangle and enters the adductor canal (Hunter's canal), a fascial tunnel in the middle third of the thigh that guides the vessel to the adductor hiatus.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Tributaries from the medial and posterior aspects of the thigh frequently unite to form which vein, which often becomes the main communication between the great and small saphenous veins?
questions.explanation: The accessory saphenous vein is a common tributary that collects blood from the posteromedial thigh. When prominent, it serves as a major anastomotic channel linking the small and great saphenous systems.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which vascular condition is defined by incompetent valves that lead to blood pooling, creating dilated and tortuous superficial vessels?
questions.explanation: Varicose veins occur when the venous valves (especially in the great saphenous vein and perforators) become incompetent, allowing blood to flow backward, pool, and distend the superficial veins.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The inferior gluteal artery primarily supplies the gluteus maximus, obturator internus, quadratus femoris, and the superior parts of which muscle group?
options: Deep lateral rotators of the hip
questions.explanation: Beyond supplying the major gluteal muscles, the inferior gluteal artery descends to provide blood to the superior origins of the hamstring muscles at the ischial tuberosity.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: During coronary angiography, a catheter is often navigated through the cardiovascular system starting from a superficial access point in the lower limb. Which artery is classically catheterized for this procedure?
questions.explanation: The femoral artery is superficial and easily palpable within the femoral triangle, making it a standard, accessible puncture site for inserting catheters destined for the aorta and coronary arteries.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: When locating the popliteal pulse, the clinician must press deeply into the popliteal fossa. What specific maneuver helps relax the tough popliteal fascia to make this pulse easier to feel?
questions.explanation: Slightly flexing the knee joint reduces tension on the popliteal fascia, allowing the clinician's fingers to press deeper into the fossa to detect the artery.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The dorsalis pedis artery supplies the tarsal bones and the dorsal aspect of the metatarsals. Where does it anatomically begin?
options: At the bifurcation of the popliteal artery
Deep to the abductor hallucis muscle
As the anterior tibial artery enters the foot
questions.correctAnswer: D. As the anterior tibial artery enters the foot
questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery changes its name to the dorsalis pedis artery exactly as it crosses the ankle joint and enters the dorsum of the foot.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: To locate the posterior tibial pulse, a clinician must palpate the medial aspect of the ankle. What is its exact relationship to the medial malleolus?
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery courses through the tarsal tunnel, and its pulse is palpable in the groove inferoposterior to the medial malleolus.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which clinical finding is considered a classic indicator of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) when assessing a patient's calf?
options: Absence of the dorsalis pedis pulse
Immediate relief of pain upon walking
questions.explanation: A positive Homan's sign (calf pain upon forced dorsiflexion of the foot) is a classic, though not definitive, clinical sign of deep vein thrombosis in the calf.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: A patient with severe peripheral arterial disease (PAD) experiences pain in their calf muscles while walking, which subsides with rest. What is the clinical term for this specific symptom?
questions.explanation: Intermittent claudication is the reproducible ischemic muscle pain that occurs during exercise and resolves with rest, typically caused by atherosclerosis in the lower limb arteries.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The anterior tibial artery descends the leg accompanied by a specific nerve. Which nerve shares this anterior compartment pathway?
questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery descends along the interosseous membrane between the tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus, accompanied by the deep fibular nerve.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which of the following structures is an essential component of the lymphatic drainage system that filters lymph directly from the deep tissues of the foot and leg before it reaches the groin?
questions.explanation: The popliteal lymph nodes receive deep lymphatic vessels from the foot and leg, acting as the first major filtration station before the lymph ascends to the deep inguinal nodes.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The lateral plantar artery is much larger than its medial counterpart. Together with a branch of the dorsalis pedis, it forms which major arterial structure in the foot?
questions.explanation: The lateral plantar artery crosses the sole of the foot to form the deep plantar arch, which is completed by the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: In addition to the lateral and medial circumflex femoral arteries, the cruciate anastomosis of the thigh receives a significant contribution from which perforating vessel?
options: First perforating artery of the deep femoral
questions.correctAnswer: D. First perforating artery of the deep femoral
questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis, which bypasses blockages between the internal iliac and femoral arteries, includes the inferior gluteal, medial/lateral circumflex femoral, and the first perforating artery.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: A surgical patient develops severe swelling and pain in the anterior leg following trauma. The diagnosis is compartment syndrome. What is the most definitive, immediate surgical treatment to prevent tissue necrosis?
questions.explanation: Compartment syndrome is treated with a fasciotomy, which involves cutting open the deep fascia to relieve the pressure and restore blood flow to the ischemic muscles.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which large nerve is situated immediately medial to the inferior gluteal artery as it descends through the gluteal region?
questions.explanation: The inferior gluteal artery leaves the pelvis inferior to the piriformis and descends on the medial side of the massive sciatic nerve.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The superficial lymphatic vessels accompanying the small saphenous vein drain into the popliteal nodes. From there, the lymph follows deep vessels that eventually terminate in which nodes?
questions.explanation: Efferent vessels from the popliteal lymph nodes ascend deep within the thigh to terminate in the deep inguinal lymph nodes.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which arteries arise from the deep plantar arch and divide near the base of the proximal phalanges to supply the adjacent digits?
questions.explanation: The deep plantar arch gives off four plantar metatarsal arteries that run distally and divide to form the plantar digital arteries for the toes.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which of the following describes the functional mechanism of venous valves in the lower limbs?
options: They actively contract to pump blood upward.
They shunt blood from deep veins into superficial veins during exercise.
Their cuplike sinuses fill from above, occluding the lumen and preventing reflux.
They open during diastole to allow blood to pool in the soleal sinuses.
questions.correctAnswer: C. Their cuplike sinuses fill from above, occluding the lumen and preventing reflux.
questions.explanation: Venous valves are endothelial cusps. When blood tries to flow backward due to gravity, the cuplike sinuses fill, forcing the cusps together to block the lumen and ensure unidirectional flow.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The fibular (peroneal) artery descends in the posterior compartment of the leg. It provides blood to the lateral compartment muscles by giving off which specific branches?
questions.explanation: The fibular artery gives off perforating branches that pierce the posterior intermuscular septum to supply the muscles of the lateral compartment.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which major lymphatic structures receive lymph directly from both the superficial and deep inguinal lymph nodes before it ascends to the lumbar trunks?
questions.explanation: Lymph from both the superficial and deep inguinal nodes drains superiorly into the external iliac lymph nodes, located along the external iliac vein in the pelvis.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The femoral artery gives off the profunda femoris artery. Where does this bifurcation typically occur?
questions.explanation: The profunda femoris (deep artery of the thigh) arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery shortly after it enters the femoral triangle.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: What is the primary vascular supply to the anterior compartment of the leg?
questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery passes through the interosseous membrane to provide the sole arterial supply to the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The medial plantar nerve accompanies the medial plantar artery. Which arterial branch accompanies the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve to form the deep plantar arch?
questions.explanation: The lateral plantar artery arches medially across the foot alongside the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve, forming the deep plantar arch.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which superficial vein of the lower limb is a direct continuation of the lateral marginal vein of the foot?
questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein begins on the lateral side of the foot as a direct upward continuation of the lateral marginal vein.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The deep veins of the lower limb are characterized by possessing more valves than the superficial veins. Why is this structural difference physiologically necessary?
options: They carry warmer blood that requires more segmentation.
They are not subjected to the musculovenous pump.
They frequently transport lymph fluid as well.
They must support a larger, heavier column of blood against gravity while relying on intermittent muscle contractions.
questions.correctAnswer: D. They must support a larger, heavier column of blood against gravity while relying on intermittent muscle contractions.
questions.explanation: Deep veins rely on the musculovenous pump. They have more valves to effectively hold the blood column against gravity between muscle contractions, preventing retrograde flow.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which specific branch of the popliteal artery supplies the inferolateral aspect of the knee joint capsule?
questions.explanation: The inferior lateral genicular artery is one of the five genicular branches of the popliteal artery, specifically targeted at the inferolateral quadrant of the knee joint.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which superficial vein runs obliquely across the anterior aspect of the medial malleolus?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein begins on the dorsum of the foot and characteristically ascends immediately anterior to the medial malleolus.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The internal pudendal artery leaves the pelvis to supply perineal structures. Does it supply the gluteal region during its brief transit through it?
options: Yes, it supplies the gluteus maximus.
Yes, it provides the main supply to the piriformis.
No, it does not supply the gluteal region.
Yes, it supplies the superior gemellus.
questions.correctAnswer: C. No, it does not supply the gluteal region.
questions.explanation: Although the internal pudendal artery enters the gluteal region through the greater sciatic foramen, it immediately exits through the lesser sciatic foramen to supply the perineum, without supplying the gluteal muscles.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: What is the primary function of the valves located within the perforating veins of the lower limb?
options: To direct blood from the deep veins into the superficial veins
To prevent blood from flowing from the deep veins back into the superficial veins
To shunt lymph into the venous system
questions.correctAnswer: C. To prevent blood from flowing from the deep veins back into the superficial veins
questions.explanation: Valves in the perforating veins ensure that blood moves only inward (superficial to deep) and prevents the high pressures generated during muscle contraction from blowing blood back into the superficial veins.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which of the following nerves travels alongside the small saphenous vein as it ascends the posterior aspect of the leg?
questions.explanation: The sural nerve is a cutaneous nerve that closely accompanies the small saphenous vein along the posterolateral aspect of the calf.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The popliteal vein is a major deep vein. It is formed at the lower border of the popliteus muscle by the union of which vessels?
questions.correctAnswer: D. Anterior and posterior tibial veins
questions.explanation: The paired anterior and posterior tibial veins (venae comitantes) ascend from the leg and unite at the lower border of the popliteus to form the single popliteal vein.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which structure forms the lateral margin of the saphenous opening, over which the great saphenous vein hooks before entering the femoral vein?
questions.explanation: The saphenous opening in the fascia lata has a sharp, crescentic lateral edge known as the falciform margin, over which the great saphenous vein passes to reach the deep femoral vein.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which set of arteries supplies the major central portions of the hamstring muscles in the posterior thigh?
options: Perforating branches of the profunda femoris
questions.correctAnswer: D. Perforating branches of the profunda femoris
questions.explanation: The perforating branches of the deep artery of the thigh (profunda femoris) pierce the adductor magnus and provide the primary blood supply to the hamstring muscles.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which artery provides the deep plantar artery that physically connects to the lateral plantar artery, completing the deep plantar arch?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery gives off the deep plantar artery, which dives between the first two metatarsals to join the lateral plantar artery and form the deep plantar arch.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: A 65-year-old patient presents with pain in the calf that reliably occurs after walking two blocks and disappears with rest. This condition, intermittent claudication, is typically caused by atherosclerosis in which vessels?
questions.explanation: Intermittent claudication of the calf is most commonly caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the superficial femoral and popliteal arteries, which restrict blood flow during exercise.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The lateral circumflex femoral artery typically divides into ascending, transverse, and descending branches. The descending branch travels distally to anastomose with which artery at the knee?
questions.explanation: The descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery courses down the lateral aspect of the thigh to join the superior lateral genicular artery in the knee's peri-articular anastomosis.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The popliteal lymph nodes filter lymph from the deep leg and foot. In addition to these deep vessels, they also receive superficial lymphatics that follow which structure?
questions.explanation: While most superficial lymphatics follow the great saphenous vein to the groin, the superficial lymphatic vessels on the lateral foot and posterior calf follow the small saphenous vein directly into the popliteal nodes.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: In a healthy standing individual, why does blood not pool excessively in the feet despite gravity?
options: Competent venous valves prevent retrograde flow and break the hydrostatic column.
Arterial pressure alone pushes the blood upward.
The deep fascia constantly contracts to squeeze the veins.
The saphenofemoral junction actively suctions blood upward.
questions.correctAnswer: A. Competent venous valves prevent retrograde flow and break the hydrostatic column.
questions.explanation: In quiet standing, gravity pulls blood down, but competent valves in the veins catch the blood, preventing retrograde flow and breaking the long hydrostatic column of blood into smaller, lower-pressure segments.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which specific artery passes through the tarsal tunnel alongside the tibial nerve to enter the sole of the foot?
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery descends the posterior leg and passes behind the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel before dividing into the medial and lateral plantar arteries.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The saphenous nerve is the longest sensory branch of the femoral nerve. Which superficial vein does it accompany as it descends through the leg?
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve emerges to the surface near the knee and accompanies the great saphenous vein down the medial side of the leg and foot.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which lymphatic vessels must be evaluated (often via sentinel node biopsy) if a patient is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma on the medial aspect of the calf?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the medial calf travels in superficial vessels accompanying the great saphenous vein, which drain directly into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which artery is the smaller of the two terminal branches of the posterior tibial artery and primarily supplies the skin and muscles on the medial side of the sole?
questions.explanation: The medial plantar artery is the smaller terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery; it supplies the medial sole and the muscles of the great toe.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: During a severe traumatic injury to the lower leg, swelling within a fascial compartment can compress arteries and nerves. What is the clinical term for this surgical emergency?
questions.explanation: Compartment syndrome occurs when increased pressure within a non-yielding fascial compartment (due to bleeding or swelling) occludes blood supply, leading to rapid muscle and nerve ischemia.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which of the following describes the relationship of the femoral vein to the femoral artery as they pass deep to the inguinal ligament?
options: The vein is lateral to the artery.
The vein is medial to the artery.
The vein is anterior to the artery.
The vein is posterior to the artery.
questions.correctAnswer: B. The vein is medial to the artery.
questions.explanation: Within the femoral sheath at the level of the inguinal ligament, the femoral vein is positioned immediately medial to the femoral artery (remember NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics, from lateral to medial).
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The anterior tibial artery continues as the dorsalis pedis artery. The dorsalis pedis artery then divides into the deep plantar artery and which other significant branch?
questions.explanation: On the dorsum of the foot, the dorsalis pedis artery divides into the deep plantar artery (which completes the plantar arch) and the arcuate artery (which arches laterally over the metatarsal bases).
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The deep veins of the lower limb are heavily valved and rely on muscle contraction for venous return. What specific arrangement of these veins maximizes the efficiency of this system?
options: They lack a tunica media entirely.
They are completely separated from the arteries by thick fascia.
They form large, single-lumen venous sinuses in the thigh.
They occur as paired venae comitantes within a shared vascular sheath with a pulsating artery.
questions.correctAnswer: D. They occur as paired venae comitantes within a shared vascular sheath with a pulsating artery.
questions.explanation: The paired venae comitantes surround the artery within a tight sheath. The expansion of the artery during systole helps physically squeeze the veins, driving blood upward.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which artery arises from the internal iliac artery, exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, and supplies the gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fasciae latae?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal artery exits the pelvis above the piriformis and divides into superficial and deep branches, supplying the upper gluteal muscles and tensor fasciae latae.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The popliteal artery bifurcates at the lower border of the popliteus muscle. If the anterior tibial artery is one branch, what is the initial trunk that forms the other branch before it splits further?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery typically divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal (tibiofibular) trunk. The tibioperoneal trunk then quickly divides into the posterior tibial and fibular arteries.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: A patient with critical limb ischemia is at high risk of developing gangrene. If conservative treatments fail, what is the ultimate surgical intervention required for a non-salvageable, gangrenous limb?
questions.explanation: When critical limb ischemia progresses to irreversible tissue death (gangrene) and revascularization is impossible, amputation of the necrotic tissue is required to prevent fatal systemic infection.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries anastomose to form a ring around the base of the femoral neck. From which larger artery do these circumflex arteries usually originate?
options: Deep artery of the thigh (profunda femoris)
questions.correctAnswer: B. Deep artery of the thigh (profunda femoris)
questions.explanation: The medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries are typically the largest branches originating from the proximal portion of the profunda femoris artery.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Which of the following vessels is NOT considered part of the deep venous system of the lower limb?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein runs within the subcutaneous tissue above the deep fascia, classifying it exclusively as a superficial vein.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: The obturator artery supplies the medial compartment of the thigh. From which major pelvic artery does it originate?
questions.explanation: The obturator artery is a branch of the internal iliac artery that exits the pelvic cavity through the obturator canal.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Plantar digital arteries supply the toes, including the nail beds. From which arteries do these digital vessels directly originate near the bases of the proximal phalanges?
questions.explanation: The plantar metatarsal arteries (arising from the deep plantar arch) travel distally and bifurcate near the proximal phalanges to become the plantar digital arteries supplying adjacent toes.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb

questions.text: Occasionally, a superficial plantar arch is present in the foot. When this occurs, it is formed by an anastomosis between the lateral plantar artery and the superficial branch of which other artery?
questions.explanation: While the deep arch is constant, a superficial plantar arch sometimes forms when the superficial branch of the medial plantar artery anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery.
questions.section: Blood Supply of the Lower Limb
